## The Museum of Unfinished Things

The Museum of Unfinished Things occupied the floor beneath a shuttered bakery on Vellum Street, between a laundromat that never seemed to have customers and a parking garage that smelled of rain trapped in concrete.

Its collection was enormous.

There were novels stopped one sentence before the climax. Paintings of landscapes with an unpainted horizon. Letters sealed but never sent. Buildings represented by foundations and scaffolding. Songs recorded with a cough halfway through the second verse. Bicycles with notes attached to the handlebars: *I was learning to be brave, but I never got the hang of it.*

Most of the museum’s visitors came at night, when admission was free and the exhibits whispered.

Mara had worked there for six years as the sole night curator. Her job was simple: keep the temperature steady, dust the artifacts, and make sure nothing wandered off.

Things did sometimes wander off.

A violin had rolled out of its case and into the ventilation system. A jar of pickles had appeared in the gift shop, though no one could identify where it had come from. Once, every clock in the museum began moving backward at exactly the same speed.

“The past is slippery,” Mara’s predecessor had told her. “If you’re not careful, it gets underfoot.”

So Mara watched carefully.

At 2:13 in the morning, the lights went out.

Not completely. A soft golden glow rose from the central gallery, where a glass case stood on a wooden pedestal. Inside was a subway map dated three years in the future. Most of its lines were gray, but one was red.

The red line began at a station marked **NOW** and ended at a station marked **TOMORROW**.

Mara stepped closer. The glass was warm. As she touched it, the case clicked open.

The map lifted itself from the pedestal and floated six inches above the floor.

Then it drifted toward the door.

Mara hesitated only long enough to grab her coat.

Outside, the city was asleep beneath a blanket of blue rain. Streets shines like black mirrors. Traffic lights changed for no one. A bus waited at the corner with its doors open, though no driver sat behind the wheel.

The map sailed down the avenue, barely a foot above the pavement.

Mara followed.

It led her past the bakery, past the laundromat, through an alley where cats watched from overturned bins. At the end of the alley stood a narrow stairway descending into darkness. The red line on the map pulsed faintly.

Down she went.

The stairs went farther than any subway station should. When Mara reached the bottom, she found herself on a platform lit by white tiles. A train waited there, empty except for a single conductor.

He was very old, with a red cap and a tired but kindly face.

“Ticket?” he asked.

Mara looked at the map. The red line still glowed between NOW and TOMORROW.

“I don’t know where I’m going,” she said.

“That’s usually the trouble,” said the conductor. “Most people buy a ticket to a place before deciding they want to arrive.”

Mara reached into her pocket. She found not money, but a brass key.

The conductor examined it. “Ah,” he said. “A ticket for the unfinished platform.”

He gestured toward the train.

The doors opened. Mara climbed aboard. The carriage had no windows, only blank walls. As the train began to move, she heard sounds from behind the walls: hammering, typing, arguing, singing, a baby crying, applause, rain striking pavement, thousands of footsteps hurrying in different directions.

“What is this line?” Mara asked.

“The line that has not been built yet.”

The train stopped after several minutes. The doors opened onto a construction site.

Cranes towered over half-built towers. Workers climbed scaffolds under violet skies. Roads stretched into fields and forests. A house stood with its roof still in pieces. A garden grew around a table where three people argued cheerfully about the color of the sky.

Near the tracks, a child was drawing a map in the dirt with a red stick.

Mara stepped off the train.

The child looked up. “You’re late,” she said.

“For what?”

“For everything.”

Around the construction site, thousands of people were working. Some carried bricks. Others carried questions. One man held a large glass jar containing a thunderstorm. A woman carried the blueprints of a house, though the house was already standing behind her, and she kept changing the windows.

A boy passed Mara carrying a pile of books with no titles.

A girl followed him carrying the courage to speak to him.

Mara understood, then, that tomorrow was not a place waiting to be discovered. It was a place being made—clumsily, bravely, one decision at a time.

The conductor leaned out of the train.

“Last train,” he called.

Mara looked back at the construction site. The unfinished things were multiplying. Half-laid roads branched like rivers. Unsent letters fluttered from wires. A vast bridge stretched halfway across a canyon, its other end lost in mist.

“I have a museum to open,” she said.

The conductor nodded. “Then take something with you.”

So Mara approached the child with the red stick.

“May I have that?” she asked.

The child frowned. “It’s the only way to draw tomorrow.”

“Then I’ll bring it back.”

“Everyone says that.”

Mara looked at the half-built city. She looked at the map glowing in her hands. She thought of all the abandoned sentences and empty horizons waiting in the museum, each one seeming less abandoned than before.

“All right,” she said. “You can have my key.”

The child took the brass key.

Mara took the red stick.

The train carried her back through the tunnels and up the stairs into the blue morning. By the time she reached the museum, dawn had painted every window gold. The floating map settled gently into its case, and a new station had appeared at the bottom of the red line.

Mara locked the door and sat beside the display.

For the first time in six years, the museum felt full of possibilities.

In the central gallery, all the unfinished things stirred.

Novels cleared their throats.

Paintings reached for their missing horizons.

And somewhere beneath the city, a train began to move along a line that had not yet been built, carrying a handful of passengers toward a morning none of them had seen.
